records.name_note: No admissible source presents a conflicting accepted name. NC State Extension, RHS, UF/IFAS, and UGA Extension all refer to this species uniformly as Ricinus communis (Family Euphorbiaceae). NC State's Plant Toolbox lists six common-name variants for the same species entry: African Wonder Tree, Castor Bean, Castor Bean Plant, Castor Oil Plant, Castor-oil Plant, and Mole Bean Plant.
records.toxicity_detail: Every part of the plant is documented as toxic, with the seeds specifically flagged as containing the lethal toxin. NC State Extension's structured Poison data names the toxic principle as "Ricin, a phytotoxalbumin, plus ricinine, an alkaloid," lists poisonous parts as "Flowers, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Seeds," and gives symptoms of "nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, weakness, colic, depression, loss of appetite, trembling, sweating, loss of coordination, difficulty breathing ... may be fatal ... May also be fatal to livestock and pets" -- explicitly covering both humans and animals, and it tags the species a problem for cats, dogs, and horses specifically. UF/IFAS's extension publication warns "the mottled seeds contain a highly poisonous agent called 'ricin' that, if inhaled or ingested, can kill animals and humans," and separately notes "Contact with the sap, flowers, leaves, or seeds has been known to cause skin rashes." RHS labels the species "TOXIC to pets if eaten" and, for humans, "TOXIC if eaten," advising gloves and protective equipment when handling it. UGA Cooperative Extension's pet-safety guide independently classifies castor bean as "Major Toxicity." Penn State Extension separately confirms it is "poisonous to humans." No admissible source disputes toxicity to pets or humans; all agree.

toxicity_detail pet-specific mechanism: the cardiac-glycoside/saponin toxic principle and its listed symptoms (irregular pulse, GI upset, coma, seizures) are documented by NC State specifically under its 'Poisonous to Humans' section. Pet toxicity itself is independently confirmed by RHS ('TOXIC to pets'), NC State's own tags ('Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses'), and Penn State Extension (toxic to dogs and cats), but none of these give pet-specific symptom detail, and only Missouri Botanical Garden's target-neutral statement ('all parts...very poisonous because they contain cardiac glycosides') ties the mechanism to the species without specifying a target.

The Penn State Extension citation for toxic_to_pets names the common name 'lily of the valley' but attaches the genus-level qualifier 'Convallaria spp.' rather than majalis specifically; treated here as applicable to this species since 'lily of the valley' in ordinary horticultural usage refers to C. majalis, but this is a genus-level rather than a strictly species-named citation.

UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu) and UGA CAES fieldreport.caes.uga.edu do not appear to host any Convallaria majalis content usable here: no UF/IFAS page naming this species was located, and the one UGA CAES table with a matching entry ('Lily-of-the-Valley / Convallaria majalis / all parts / nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, irregular heartbeat and pulse, mental confusion') is explicitly titled 'Ornamental Plants Reported To Be Toxic When Ingested by Humans' -- a human-only table -- so it was not used to support toxic_to_pets or toxicity_detail.

Clemson HGIC has no dedicated Convallaria majalis species profile; the two Clemson citations used here are list entries on general factsheets (Growing Perennials; Plants for Damp or Wet Areas), not narrative species text.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: Verified by direct fetch of https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/convallaria-majalis/: the cardiac-glycoside/saponin toxic-principle text and the full symptom list ('Irregular and slow pulse, abdominal pain and diarrhea, low blood pressure, disorientation, coma, seizures') sit entirely under NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading -- confirmed word-for-word -- with no parallel pet-toxicity narrative section anywhere on the page. Pet toxicity on that page is signaled only by bare 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' tags, carrying zero mechanism or symptom detail. So the mechanism/symptom paragraph the record installs into toxicity_detail is, per audit check #3, content copied from a human-toxicity section, not verified animal-toxicity content -- no admissible source ties these specific symptoms or severity to dogs, cats, or horses. The record's inline caveat ('filed under NC State's Poisonous to Humans section, not a pets-specific section') accurately discloses this but doesn't cure it: a reader of a pet-safety field could still take detailed human clinical symptoms (coma, seizures, abdominal pain) as what to watch for in a poisoned pet. Notably the same record's own unknowns list shows the researcher recognizes this exact failure mode -- it explicitly excludes a UGA CAES table from supporting toxic_to_pets because that table was titled 'toxic ... to Humans' -- making it inconsistent to then transcribe NC State's human-only symptom block into toxicity_detail anyway. The field should be pared back to what's actually animal-relevant: MOBOT's target-unspecified 'contain cardiac glycosides' statement, plus a note that no admissible source gives pet-specific symptoms, rather than the full human poisoning-symptom transcript.

records.name_note: The given name is the currently accepted binomial. RHS's own "Name Status" field for this page reads "Correct." NC State lists two retired synonyms — "Previously known as: Taxus aurea Taxus columnaris" — neither of which conflicts with Taxus baccata as the accepted name. No admissible source proposed a different accepted binomial for this species, so there is no genuine naming conflict to document here.
records.toxicity_detail: The seeds are specifically documented as the poisonous part of the fruit: NC State's general (non-human-specific) fruit description states that female plants "bear single seeds that are partially enclosed by arils," and adds plainly, "The seeds are poisonous." NC State's more detailed toxic-principle and symptom information (taxines/taxiphyllin; bark, leaves, seeds, and stems listed as poison parts) exists on the same species page but is nested specifically under a "Poisonous to Humans" heading rather than a pets-specific one, so it was deliberately not folded into this pets-facing detail — see unknowns.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a target ambient daytime or nighttime temperature range for this outdoor landscape tree; NC State, RHS, and Missouri Botanical Garden describe only hardiness-zone and general climate tolerance, not a controlled temperature target.

chill_damage_f: only survival/hardiness-zone data exists -- NC State USDA Hardiness Zones 6a-7b, Missouri Botanical Garden Zone 6-7, and RHS Hardiness rating H7 -- with no admissible source giving a specific Fahrenheit damage-onset figure; NC State's prose says only that the plant is 'intolerant of...extremely hot or cold temperatures' and should be sheltered from 'cold winter winds,' with no number given. Per the field's own definition (damage-onset, not survival), this is expected to be null for a hardy landscape tree and was not forced from the zone/hardiness-rating data.

cool_rest_note: no admissible source frames a deliberate temperature-based winter rest period for this species; it is described only as a broadleaf evergreen conifer that should be sheltered from winter wind.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source -- all three primary sources describe only outdoor landscape/garden conditions, with no ambient-humidity guidance.
light_fc_min, light_fc_good: no admissible source gives an indoor footcandle figure; sources give only outdoor sun-exposure position categories (full sun / partial shade / full shade).

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's 'Partial Shade' category is itself defined as 2-6 hours, but this species is also documented as tolerating full sun and even full shade without qualification by all three primary sources (NC State, RHS, and MOBOT's 'Tolerant of full shade'), so presenting 6 as a sun-hours ceiling would incorrectly imply a cap on the endorsed full-sun value that no source actually states; left null rather than force this fit.

soil_base: no admissible source uses a substrate/potting-mix category label for this species; all three primary sources describe only in-ground landscape soil texture and pH tolerance for what is documented exclusively as a large outdoor tree/hedge/screen plant (30-60 ft per NC State and MOBOT; 'Higher than 12 metres' per RHS), never a container or potted subject. None of the fixed soil_base enum values was confidently supported by the sources' own words, so this was left null rather than forced into 'garden_bed' on inference alone.

water_regime: NC State ('Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist'; 'intolerant of wet or poorly drained sites') and Missouri Botanical Garden ('Water: Medium'; 'evenly moist...with excellent drainage') both pair moisture with a strong drainage requirement without describing a dry-down cycle, while RHS gives only 'Well-drained' with no moisture-frequency language at all. None of the three sources' wording maps cleanly onto a single schema water_regime category (keep_moist vs. dry_surface_between) without either overstating a drainage-intolerant-of-wet plant as wanting constant moisture, or dropping the explicit moisture requirement -- left null rather than guessed.

water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a numeric watering-interval, soil-moisture-check depth, or dormancy-duration figure for this species; only qualitative moisture/drainage guidance was found.
fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: no admissible source addresses a fertilizing schedule for this species at all.

soil_ph is well supported by NC State's specific categorical range ('Soil pH: Neutral (6.0-8.0)'), but note RHS separately describes this species more broadly as tolerant of 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' soil with no numeric bounds given -- not a numeric conflict, but the broader RHS tolerance statement was not used to override NC State's specific target range.

toxicity_detail deliberately excludes NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block (Poison Severity: High; Poison Symptoms including dry mouth, vomiting, irregular heart rhythms, cardiac/respiratory failure; Poison Toxic Principle taxines and taxiphyllin; Poison Part Bark/Leaves/Seeds/Stems) because that whole block sits nested directly under a 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading on the live page, not a pets-specific one -- confirmed by direct fetch of the page structure. One sentence inside that same block does broaden past humans ('The plant is highly poisonous and can be fatal to humans, domestic animals, and livestock'), but given the ambiguous scoping this was not used for toxicity_detail either; toxic_to_pets itself is instead independently and cleanly supported by NC State's parallel (non-nested) 'Problem for Cats'/'Problem for Dogs'/'Problem for Horses' tags and by RHS's separate bare statement 'TOXIC to pets if eaten.'

No admissible source explicitly states that the fleshy red aril itself is non-toxic/safe to eat. NC State's Fruit Description names the seeds specifically as poisonous, and its (human-scoped) Poison Part list of Bark/Leaves/Seeds/Stems omits fruit/aril, and its Wildlife Value note ('Birds eat the fleshy arils and disperse the seeds') describes birds consuming the aril with no harm mentioned -- but none of this rises to a direct, admissible-source claim that the aril flesh is non-toxic, so toxicity_detail states only what is directly supported (the seeds are the documented poisonous fruit component) rather than asserting aril safety.

Clemson Cooperative Extension HGIC: searched hgic.clemson.edu directly and via web search; no dedicated Taxus baccata or general yew care/toxicity factsheet was found. Only an unrelated 'Leaf & Needle Drop' factsheet mentions yew in passing regarding seasonal needle shedding, with no care or toxicity content specific to this species, so it was not used.

UF/IFAS Extension: UF/IFAS's dedicated Taxus baccata publication (ENH-782/ST624, 'Taxus baccata: English Yew') was located via search, but as of this research both edis.ifas.ufl.edu/st624 and ask.ifas.ufl.edu/st624 return 'The publication you requested is no longer available on Ask IFAS' (confirmed by direct browser navigation, not just an automated fetch failure), so it could not be used as a live, quotable citation.

University of Maryland Extension: no dedicated Taxus baccata/English yew plant-profile page was found; only pest-management factsheets (black vine weevil, cottony camellia scale, deer damage to ornamentals) list yew/Taxus as a host or browse plant in passing, with no care or toxicity content usable for this record's fields.

UGA Cooperative Extension: two relevant publications were found -- Circular 1245 'Keep Your Pets Safe Around Plants' (lists 'Taxus spp.' under 'Major Toxicity: May result in serious illness or death if ingested') and Circular 957 'Poisonous Plants in the Landscape' (lists, in a table of plants toxic to HUMANS specifically, 'Yew** / Taxus spp. / berries, foliage / foliage more toxic than berries, death can be sudden without symptoms') -- but neither names the species Taxus baccata specifically; both use the genus label 'Taxus spp.' Per the rule against inferring toxicity from genus/family alone, neither was used as a citation, even though both are consistent with the NC State- and RHS-sourced toxic_to_pets=true finding, and Circular 957's foliage-vs-berries note is broadly consistent with (though not used to independently confirm) the seed/fruit distinction NC State documents at the species level.

Penn State Extension: only one substantive mention of this species was found, a single sentence in a general 'Growin' of the Green' color-in-landscaping article ('Classic English yews (Taxus baccata) are popular evergreen landscape plants...'), with no dedicated care or toxicity page for this species; used only as minor corroboration for is_houseplant/landscape framing.

is_houseplant: no admissible source contains an explicit sentence stating this species is 'not grown indoors.' The false determination rests on the combination of exclusively outdoor-landscape/hedge/topiary framing and full mature tree dimensions (30-60 ft per NC State and MOBOT; 'Higher than 12 metres' per RHS) across all three primary sources, with zero container or indoor-culture guidance found anywhere, rather than on one direct disclaiming quote.

NC State does tag the species '#bonsai' and includes a photo captioned 'As bonsai,' but bonsai culture for this species is practiced outdoors (pines need winter dormancy/cold exposure and full sun), and no source frames it as an indoor or long-term container plant, so is_houseplant is false with no container-specific carve-out.

records.name_note: Platycerium bifurcatum is the currently accepted binomial — RHS lists its "Name Status" as "Correct." NC State Extension notes the species was previously classified under two older synonyms, Acrostichum bifurcatum and Alcicornium bifurcatum. Separately, two admissible sources flag a trade/labeling confusion rather than a true naming conflict: Missouri Botanical Garden states the species is "Synonymous with and sometimes sold as P. alcicorne," and RHS's own synonym field lists "Platycerium alcicorne misapplied" — i.e., a related but distinct species name that nursery stock of P. bifurcatum is sometimes mistakenly sold under. No admissible source disputes P. bifurcatum itself as the correct accepted name.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: Clemson HGIC's staghorn-fern row gives "Night temperatures of 50 to 55 °F and day temperatures of 68 to 72 °F," but a systematic check of every fern entry on the same Indoor Ferns page found this exact figure reused verbatim across at least seven different fern species (Holly Fern, Kangaroo Paw Fern, Boston/Sword Fern, Rabbit's Foot Fern, Sword Brake Fern, and Crested Spider Brake Fern, in addition to Staghorn Fern) — clearly a generic "typical houseplant fern" default rather than staghorn-specific data, so it was not used per the boilerplate-detection guidance.

chill_damage_f: only survival/hardiness-zone data exists — NC State USDA zones 9a-13b, Missouri Botanical Garden "Winter hardy to USDA Zone 9-12," and RHS Hardiness H1B ("can be grown outside in the summer (10 - 15°C)", i.e. not frost-hardy at all) — none of which is a damage-onset figure, so left null as expected for a tender tropical epiphyte.

humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: Clemson, RHS, and Missouri Botanical Garden all describe a qualitative "high"/"very high"/"humid" need, but none gives a percentage specific to staghorn fern (Clemson's Maidenhair Fern entry on the same page gives "about 50 percent," but that number belongs to a different species on the same table and was not borrowed).
light_fc_min/light_fc_good: no admissible source gives a footcandle figure; all describe only categorical light (dappled sunlight/partial shade/bright indirect or filtered light/avoid direct sun).

soil_drainage: NC State's structured field reads simply "Good Drainage" with no further qualifier, applied to a plant that per the record's own soil_base is not actually grown in soil but mounted/potted in bark or sphagnum moss — genuinely ambiguous between the schema's "fast" and "moderate" categories for that kind of medium, so left null rather than guessed.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State tags "Soil pH: Acid (<6.0)" but this is the site's standard soil-based categorical field, and per this task's own species note pH fields may not meaningfully apply to a fern mounted in bark/sphagnum moss rather than grown in soil. No admissible source gives an actual pH reading for the sphagnum moss/bark/peat growing medium itself, so left null rather than repurpose a generic soil-pH tag onto a non-soil medium.

soil_base is supported (orchid_bark, from NC State's "epiphytic orchid or sphagnum moss mixture" and Missouri Botanical Garden's "epiphytic or sphagnum fern mix") but note this is an approximation: multiple sources (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, UGA) describe an equally valid alternative culture method — mounting bare-root on a wood or cork bark slab with sphagnum moss or peat moss packed around the crown, tied or wired in place, with no pot or bark-chip medium at all. The chosen enum value best fits the potted-culture option; the bark-mount option doesn't map to any schema soil_base category.

water_regime: genuine cross-source conflict on a harm-capable field, left null. Clemson states "Keep the material on which the plant grows moist at all times" (continuous moisture, no drying cycle implied). NC State ("allowing the roots to dry slightly between waterings but never letting them dry out completely") and Missouri Botanical Garden ("allowing roots to dry slightly between waterings. Roots must never be allowed to dry out.") both instead describe a cyclical slight-drying pattern. RHS adds a third framing, a seasonal-intensity model rather than a dry-down cycle: "water freely" when in growth, "Water sparingly in winter." UGA adds a fourth data point that is frequent rather than dry-down oriented: "Water everyday in summer. Mist daily inside during winter." None of the schema's four regime categories captures all of these without contradicting at least one source.

water_dry_down_target/water_check_depth_cm/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: left null together with water_regime given the conflict described above; no admissible source gives a numeric watering-interval or moisture-check-depth figure that all sources agree on.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: genuine conflict. RHS instructs to "apply a balanced liquid fertiliser monthly" during active growth (in its UK under-glass cultivation context), while UGA states the plant "Does not need much fertilization" and recommends only an annual top-dressing of the growing medium ("once a year, add top dressing of the soil mixture between flat frond and slab") — roughly a twelve-fold difference in frequency, and describing a different practice (medium top-dressing vs. liquid feed). Neither was adopted as a general schedule; no source names specific calendar months or a dilution strength.

cool_rest_note: RHS's only cold-season note is "Water sparingly in winter" — a watering-reduction instruction, not a temperature-based rest/dormancy description, so it was not force-fit into this field; it is instead reflected as one of the conflicting data points under water_regime.

toxicity_detail: left null because toxic_to_pets is false per NC State's structured tags ("non-toxic for cats"/"non-toxic for dogs"/"non-toxic for horses"/"pet friendly"), with no conflicting admissible source found — RHS's page for this species carries no toxicity tag at all (unlike RHS pages for toxic species, which explicitly state "TOXIC to pets"), and Clemson, Missouri Botanical Garden, and UGA do not address toxicity for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max — removed on audit: The value 6 is drawn from a single NC State citation ("Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)") -- verified word-for-word against the live page. But UGA Extension's B737 Growing Ferns, cited elsewhere in this same record for outdoor_sun_exposure, carries a species-specific header "Staghorn Fern / Platycerium bifurcatum" (confirmed not boilerplate -- the neighboring Sword Fern and Rabbit's Foot Fern entries on the same page have distinctly different light text) with the instruction "Bright light but avoid direct sun." That is a direct, admissible, species-specific statement that conflicts with treating 6 hours of direct sun as safe for this plant. The schema's own comment on this field (models.py: "direct-beam tolerance... that difference is what scorches leaves") marks it as a harm-capable field. No second, independent, unproblematic citation cleanly corroborates the number 6 -- RHS gives no hour figure at all, and UGA's species-specific guidance points the other way. Per the audit's conflict rule, this should have been left null rather than adopting NC State's literal upper bound over a conflicting same-species source.

normalizations: 2026-08-23: eighth batch of the "blind spots" pass. Three high-priority safety gaps, all confirmed toxic_to_pets=true with strong, consistent multi-source support: Castor Bean (ricin, one of the most toxic ornamentals commonly grown -- 6 sources agree with zero dispute, a clean pass with 0 fields removed), Lily of the Valley (cardiac glycosides, an unassuming spring groundcover that is actually severely toxic), and English Yew (taxine alkaloids, an extremely common evergreen hedge plant). Eastern White Pine is a TRUE pine (genus Pinus), completing a naming-trap thread already run through this catalog for Norfolk Island Pine (Araucaria heterophylla, not a true pine, in b24). Its toxic_to_pets landed null -- true pines are not generally documented as toxic in extension literature, and no admissible source addresses it either way for this species, so null is the honest answer rather than an assumed false.

Lily of the Valley's toxicity_detail was correctly pared back after the audit found the record's own symptom narrative ("coma, seizures, abdominal pain") was lifted from NC State's human-toxicity section -- the record's own reasoning had already excluded a UGA table on the identical human-vs-pet distinction elsewhere in the same document, making the toxicity_detail lapse an inconsistency the audit caught by holding the record to its own stated standard. toxic_to_pets=true itself is untouched and remains well-supported independently.
